The patient presents for a health check.

He reports no significant medical issues in the past, with the exception of occasional knee pain, which is not severe. He is not on any regular medications and has no known allergies. He has been a non-smoker for about 10 years, having previously smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 15 years. He consumes alcohol 2 to 3 times a week but is mindful not to overindulge. He expresses concern about his health, noting that it has been some time since his last checkup. He has been making efforts to improve his diet by reducing his intake of fried foods and sausages. His current physical activity is limited to walking, but he expresses interest in joining a local walking group. He acknowledges the need for increased physical activity. He has been attempting to reduce his alcohol consumption but finds it challenging due to social circumstances. He is hesitant about starting medication but is open to trying it. He reports no symptoms of diabetes, such as frequent urination, and notes that his weight has remained stable. He reports no feelings of depression or anxiety and generally maintains a positive mood. He values spending time with his family and grandchildren.

Laboratory Studies

Total cholesterol is 5.8 mmol/L. Fasting glucose is 6.2 mmol/L.
healthCheck.assessmentAndPlan:
1. Health maintenance.

His BMI, blood pressure, and cholesterol levels are slightly elevated, increasing his risk of developing heart disease over the next decade. Given his family history and fasting glucose levels, there is a potential risk for diabetes, although he currently exhibits no symptoms such as frequent urination or weight loss. His weight has remained stable. He is advised to adopt lifestyle modifications, including dietary changes and increased physical activity. The DASH diet, which emphasises fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and reduced salt intake, is recommended. A low-dose statin, specifically atorvastatin, is suggested to manage his cardiovascular risk factors considering his family history. A repeat blood test is recommended in a few months to monitor his fasting glucose levels and HbA1c. An eye check is also suggested as it has been a couple of years since his last one. Information on the DASH diet and local walking groups will be provided to encourage him to stay active.

Follow-up

The patient will follow up in 3 months to recheck his blood pressure, cholesterol, and glucose levels.

medicalContent.referralLetter:
Dear NAME,

Ellis Turner has presented with symptoms indicative of a viral upper respiratory infection. He has been experiencing a scratchy throat, sneezing, a persistent dry cough, fever reaching up to 38.8 °C, mild headache, muscle aches, and shortness of breath, particularly when coughing. His symptoms began approximately 4 days ago. He has been managing His fever with paracetamol and staying hydrated.

Ellis has no significant past medical history, no known drug allergies, and is not on any regular medication except for the contraceptive pill, Microgynon. He does not smoke and drinks alcohol socially.

On examination, Ellis appeared alert but flushed, with a temperature of 38.5 °C, a pulse of 92, a respiratory rate of 20 breaths/min, and an oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. His throat was mildly red without pus, His chest was clear with no wheezing or crackles, and His heart sounds were normal. There were no signs of sinusitis or neck stiffness.

Given the clinical findings, I have advised Ellis to continue taking acetaminophen to manage fever and to rest as much as possible. An over-the-counter cough syrup such as Ventolin may be beneficial for His cough, particularly at night. Antibiotics are not necessary at this stage. He has also been recommended to take a few days off work to fully rest and recover.

I am referring Ellis to your care for further evaluation and management of His viral upper respiratory infection. If He experiences increased breathlessness, persistent fever beyond a week, or the onset of chest pain, He has been advised to return for a follow-up visit or seek immediate medical attention at the emergency department.

Thank you for your attention to this referral.

Yours sincerely,

Dr. Smith, General Practitioner, GMC 123456, 20/11/2025
medicalContent.letterToGp:
Diagnosis/Problem list:
- Blepharitis
- Routine eye examination



Management plan:
- Hot compresses twice daily for 5 to 10 minutes each time
- Lubricating drops three times daily: once after the hot compresses or immediately after inserting contact lenses, once around midday, and once in the late afternoon or before bedtime
- Follow-up appointment with the contact lens team in 3 months
- Routine eye examination in 2 years or sooner if any issues arise



Dear NAME



Your patient attended a consultation on 21/11/2025 for a routine eye checkup and reported experiencing dry eyes for the past 6 months.



The patient described symptoms of itchy and scratchy eyes, particularly towards the end of the day. These symptoms improve upon removing contact lenses. The patient wears daily disposable multifocal contact lenses and has been using them daily for about 10 hours each day. The patient’s vision has improved with the recent change in contact lenses, and there are no issues with the current glasses, which are 2 years old. The patient does not drive and has no significant family history of eye conditions or diabetes.



The patient underwent an eye scan, which showed normal results, indicating healthy eyes. The clinical examination confirmed a diagnosis of blepharitis, characterised by a deficiency in the oil layer of the tear film, leading to compensatory excessive tear production and dry eye symptoms.



We discussed the treatment options, including the use of hot compresses and lubricating drops. The patient was advised to use hot compresses twice daily for 5 to 10 minutes each time and to apply lubricating drops three times daily: once after the hot compresses or immediately after inserting contact lenses, once around midday, and once in the late afternoon or before bedtime. It was explained that these measures should significantly improve symptoms within 10 days. A follow-up appointment with the contact lens team is scheduled for 3 months from now.



Our next step will be to review the patient’s progress in 3 months with the contact lens team and to conduct a routine eye examination in 2 years, or sooner if any issues arise.



Yours sincerely,



CLINICIAN_NAME, ROLE, PROFESSIONAL_ID, 21/11/2025



Glossary:
- Blepharitis: Inflammation of the eyelid margins, often causing dry eyes and irritation.
- Lubricating drops: Eye drops used to moisten the eyes and relieve dryness.
- Hot compresses: A warm, damp cloth applied to the eyes to help open oil glands and improve tear film quality.
